query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An AI-based process-parameter optimization applied to a mechanical alloying plus spark plasma sintering (SPS) route can enable large-scale synthesis of RHEA–Cu composites with stable, uniform microstructures despite the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and copper.
generation.material_initial_state: Mixed elemental or pre-alloyed RHEA powders combined with copper powders, prone to segregation due to positive mixing enthalpies in conventional high-temperature processing.
generation.intervention: Adopt data-driven parameter selection for mechanical alloying (e.g., milling speed/time, ball-to-powder ratio) and SPS (e.g., heating rate, maximum temperature, hold time) to achieve uniform dispersion and control interdiffusion at larger scales.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled environments to minimize contamination during mechanical alloying, followed by short high-temperature SPS cycles optimized via machine learning for reproducible scale-up.
generation.structural_mediator: Powder-based mixture of refractory elements with copper, mechanically alloyed into a homogeneous feedstock to suppress segregation and heterogeneities during sintering.
generation.mechanism: Precisely tuned process time and temperature reduce uncontrolled interdiffusion and phase separation, while the rapid sintering kinetics of SPS promotes uniform densification and fine-grained microstructure retention.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced compositional segregation and stable microstructures suitable for demanding nuclear-reactor environments, with improved mechanical and thermal properties.
generation.baseline: Conventional melting or high-temperature techniques often lead to microstructural inhomogeneities and excessive segregation of copper in refractory alloys due to large positive mixing enthalpies.
generation.boundary: Applicability is contingent on sufficiently accurate data for machine learning parameter optimization; the approach’s success may vary with different refractory–Cu compositions or extreme industrial scales.
generation.uncertainty: Exact phase evolution and long-term stability under prototypical nuclear-reactor conditions require further detailed experimentation and validation at scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject a range of RHEA–Cu powder blends to mechanical alloying and SPS with different time–temperature–pressure conditions; half of the trials are optimized via machine learning, and the remainder uses trial-and-error engineering limits.
measurements: Microstructural analysis by SEM/EDS (uniformity, phase distribution)
Mechanical property testing (hardness, compressive yield strength)
High-temperature exposure tests for thermal stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no improvement in microstructural uniformity and mechanical properties is observed, or if excessive microsegregation and phase separation occur in the machine-learning-optimized condition, then the proposed hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. For example, Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 and V20Nb20Mo20Ta20 refractory HEAs produced by vacuum arc-melting exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1058 MPa and 1246 MPa, respectively, with plasticities of less than 2% at room temperature [ [5] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. decision.trend: Early work on refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) relied on conventional melting and casting methods, but researchers soon adopted powder-based approaches—particularly mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS)—to achieve finer microstructures and incorporate hard secondary phases. Papers PMC5978046 and PMC7513042 both used these routes successfully for RHEAs, showing that short, high-temperature SPS cycles help retain uniform microstructures and mitigate unwanted interdiffusion and phase segregation despite high mixing enthalpies. Nonetheless, while these methods enable formation of stable RHEA composites, challenges remain in scaling to larger volumes and systematically controlling processing parameters for new multi-component systems (including those with strong positive mixing enthalpies, such as RHEA–Cu).
decision.unsolved: For RHEA–Cu composites, achieving a stable interface and uniform mixing remains difficult because of copper’s positive heat of mixing with refractory elements. Conventional high-temperature processes can lead to severe segregation or inhomogeneous reactions, especially at scale. Methods such as mechanical alloying plus spark plasma sintering offer promise, but identifying robust processing windows that accommodate copper’s immiscibility and yield stable microstructures over large volumes requires further refinement and predictive guidance.
decision.lever: Implement an AI-driven process-parameter optimization to guide the mechanical alloying plus SPS route for RHEA–Cu powders. Key parameters include ball-milling speed and duration, SPS heating rate, maximum temperature, and hold time, all optimized via machine learning to maintain uniform dispersion and mitigate segregation during scale-up.
decision.why: Because the immiscibility of copper and refractory elements demands precise tuning of processing conditions, a data-driven approach can efficiently navigate the vast parameter space, facilitating robust scale-up and stable composite microstructures.
